decks.name: Anatomy I: Meninges, CSF & Vessels (Board Review)

cards.rueckseite:
Two layers intracranially: **outer periosteal** (adheres to calvaria, ends at foramen magnum) and **inner meningeal** (continues as the spinal dura, ends at **S2**). The spinal dura therefore has only one layer → true epidural space in the spine.
Filum terminale (pia) continues from S2 as the coccygeal ligament.

Pial band on the lateral cord **midway between dorsal and ventral roots**, attaching to arachnoid/dura. Surgical landmark: cutting it allows cord rotation for anterolateral access; the anterolateral (spinothalamic) tract lies just anterior.

**Supratentorial:** trigeminal: V1 anterior fossa (and tentorium via tentorial nerve), V2 middle fossa, V3 middle fossa/posterior parts.
**Infratentorial:** upper cervical roots (**C2–C3**) and **CN X**.
Explains referred pain: supratentorial → frontal/periorbital, infratentorial → occipital/neck.

cards.text: CSF production ≈ {{c1::0.35 mL/min (≈ 20 mL/h, ≈ 450–500 mL/day)}}; total volume ≈ {{c2::150 mL}}, of which {{c3::~25 mL}} are in the ventricles. About {{c4::70%}} comes from the choroid plexus.

cards.rueckseite:
**Decrease:** acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor), furosemide, norepinephrine (sympathetic), steroids; raised ICP does **not** substantially reduce production.
**Increase:** volatile anesthetics, CO₂ (hypercapnia), choroid plexus papilloma.
Absorption is passive, **pressure-dependent**, via arachnoid granulations (open when ICP exceeds venous pressure by ~3–6 cm H₂O).
CSF below a complete spinal block (loculated lumbar sac): **xanthochromia, very high protein, spontaneous clotting** (fibrinogen).

Adults/older children **< 10–15 mmHg**; young children 3–8 mmHg; infants 1.5–6 mmHg.
Monro–Kellie volumes: brain ~1,500 mL, blood ~150 mL, CSF ~150 mL.

**BBB:** tight junctions of **capillary endothelium** (main), few pinocytotic vesicles, astrocyte foot processes. Lipid-soluble substances, O₂, CO₂, H₂O pass freely; proteins, L-glucose do not; D-glucose via carrier.
**Blood–CSF barrier:** **choroid plexus epithelium** tight junctions (its capillaries are fenestrated).

Lack a BBB (fenestrated capillaries): **OVLT**, **subfornical organ**, **median eminence**, **neurohypophysis**, **pineal gland**, **area postrema**.
- Area postrema: chemoreceptor trigger zone (emesis), floor of 4th ventricle, **only paired** CVO
- **Subcommissural organ:** the only CVO **with** an intact BBB

cards.notiz: CNBR p. 8. Brain = 2% of body weight, 15–20% of cardiac output, 20% of O₂.

cards.rueckseite:
"**SALFOPS Max**": **S**uperior thyroid, **A**scending pharyngeal, **L**ingual, **F**acial, **O**ccipital, **P**osterior auricular, **S**uperficial temporal, **Max**illary (→ middle meningeal, accessory meningeal).
Ascending pharyngeal supplies CN IX–XI and anastomoses with the vertebral artery; occipital artery also anastomoses with the vertebral artery.

cards.vorderseite: Cavernous sinus: contents and their positions
cards.rueckseite:
**Lateral wall** (superior → inferior): **CN III, IV, V1, V2**.
**Within the sinus:** **ICA** (with sympathetic plexus) and **CN VI**, which lies **inferolateral to the ICA** (free in the sinus, hence first affected by cavernous lesions/aneurysms).
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 10. V2 is variably described as in the lower lateral wall.

cards.rueckseite:
- **Meningohypophyseal trunk** (posterior genu): tentorial artery (**Bernasconi–Cassinari**), inferior hypophyseal artery (neurohypophysis), dorsal meningeal artery (CN VI, clivus)
- **Inferolateral trunk:** cavernous sinus wall, CN III, IV, VI, gasserian ganglion; anastomoses with ECA (foramen rotundum artery, MMA)
- **McConnell capsular arteries** (~28%): pituitary

Usually the **first intradural ICA branch** (~90%), below the anterior clinoid; runs **inferolateral to the optic nerve** in the optic canal, then crosses over it in the orbit. Branches: **central retinal artery**, ciliary, lacrimal, ethmoidal, supraorbital, supratrochlear.
Rarely arises from the **MMA** → risk of blindness when embolizing the MMA.
Ophthalmic aneurysms point **superiorly/superomedially** toward the optic nerve.

Arises from the **posteromedial** ICA just beyond the ophthalmic artery; supplies **adenohypophysis/infundibulum (portal system), optic chiasm undersurface** and optic nerve. Superior hypophyseal aneurysms point **inferomedially** (can mimic pituitary lesions, cause visual loss).

cards.vorderseite: Posterior communicating artery: perforators and variants
cards.rueckseite:
Runs posteriorly **above/medial to CN III** to P1. Perforators supply anterior thalamus, posterior hypothalamus, subthalamic nucleus, posterior limb of the internal capsule.
Variants: hypoplastic (~30%); **fetal PCA (~20%)**: PComm as large as PCA, P1 hypoplastic → PCA territory from ICA. **Infundibulum:** funnel-shaped origin < 2–3 mm, vessel arising from its apex.
PComm aneurysms project toward **CN III** (pupil-involving palsy).

cards.vorderseite: Anterior choroidal artery: territory and syndrome
cards.rueckseite:
Arises from the ICA distal to PComm; cisternal segment then enters the temporal horn at the **plexal point** (choroidal fissure).
Supplies: **posterior limb of the internal capsule**, optic tract, **lateral geniculate body**, globus pallidus (medial), uncus/amygdala/hippocampus, choroid plexus of the temporal horn.
Occlusion: **contralateral hemiplegia, hemianesthesia, homonymous hemianopia**.

Largest medial lenticulostriate artery; arises from **proximal A2 (~ACommA level)** and runs back along A1 into the anterior perforated substance.
Supplies: **head of caudate, anterior limb of the internal capsule**, anterior putamen/globus pallidus.
Injury: contralateral **face and arm weakness** (± aphasia if dominant).

**A1** (precommunicating; medial lenticulostriates to chiasm, anterior hypothalamus) → **A2** (postcommunicating to pericallosal–callosomarginal junction; Heubner, orbitofrontal, frontopolar) → **A3+** distal.
ACommA aneurysms arise where the **dominant A1** meets the ACommA and point **away** from it. The pericallosal–callosomarginal junction is the second most common ACA aneurysm site.

cards.vorderseite: MCA segments and lateral lenticulostriate arteries
cards.rueckseite:
**M1** horizontal (to bifurcation ~50% / trifurcation ~25%) → **M2** insular → **M3** opercular → **M4** cortical.
Lateral lenticulostriates (2–15) from M1 supply putamen, lateral globus pallidus, superior internal capsule, caudate head/body: typical site of **hypertensive hemorrhage**.

**P1** (basilar tip → PComm; interpeduncular cistern; thalamoperforators incl. artery of Percheron) → **P2** ambient (PComm → dorsal midbrain; medial/lateral posterior choroidal, thalamogeniculate) → **P3** quadrigeminal → **P4** cortical (calcarine, parieto-occipital).
Complete ("textbook") in only **~25%**; ~50% have posterior variations. Components: ACommA, A1s, ICAs, PCommAs, P1s, basilar tip.

From subclavian, enters the **C6 transverse foramen** (~90%), ascends to C2, turns lateral, runs posteriorly on the C1 arch (sulcus arteriosus), pierces the dura at the foramen magnum.
Dominance: **left ~50%**, right ~25%, equal ~25%. Left VA from the aorta in ~5%. Can **terminate in PICA**.

Segments: anterior medullary → lateral medullary (CN IX–XI) → **tonsillomedullary** (caudal loop) → **telovelotonsillar** (cranial loop) → cortical. Supplies lateral medulla, inferior vermis, tonsils, inferior hemisphere, choroid of the 4th ventricle.
Occlusion (or vertebral artery): **lateral medullary (Wallenberg) syndrome**.

cards.vorderseite: AICA and SCA: relationships and supply
cards.rueckseite:
**AICA:** crosses CN VI, loops near the internal auditory canal (**CN VII/VIII**), gives the **labyrinthine artery**; supplies inferolateral pons, middle cerebellar peduncle, flocculus. Occlusion → ipsilateral deafness, facial palsy.
**SCA:** runs around the pontomesencephalic junction **below the tentorium and CN III**, near CN IV and V (classic trigeminal neuralgia vessel); supplies superior cerebellum and deep nuclei.

zeilen: Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral hemiplegia
Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral tremor/ataxia (± hemiparesis)
Dorsal tegmentum (red nucleus, superior cerebellar peduncle)
Ipsilateral CN III palsy + contralateral ataxia
Upgaze palsy, light–near dissociation, convergence–retraction nystagmus
Recurrent artery of Heubner, MCA lateral lenticulostriates

cards.rueckseite:
Superior sagittal sinus → usually **right transverse sinus** (~60%). Straight sinus (vein of Galen + inferior sagittal sinus) → usually **left transverse sinus**. Transverse → sigmoid → jugular bulb → IJV.
Cavernous sinus → superior petrosal (to transverse–sigmoid junction) and **inferior petrosal sinus (to IJV)**.

**Vein of Trolard** (superior anastomotic): sylvian → **superior sagittal sinus** ("Trolard = top").
**Vein of Labbé** (inferior anastomotic): sylvian → **transverse sinus** ("Labbé = lower"); injury during temporal approaches → **venous infarction**/aphasia.
Superficial middle cerebral (sylvian) vein → cavernous/sphenoparietal sinus.

**Thalamostriate + septal veins** meet at the **venous angle** (foramen of Monro) → **internal cerebral veins** (in the velum interpositum, roof of the 3rd ventricle) + **basal veins of Rosenthal** (ambient cistern) → **vein of Galen** → with inferior sagittal sinus → **straight sinus**.

- **Occipital** and **ascending pharyngeal** ↔ **vertebral** (C1–C3)
- Ascending pharyngeal ↔ petrous/cavernous ICA
- **Facial (angular)** ↔ **ophthalmic** (dorsal nasal)
- **MMA** ↔ ophthalmic (via ethmoidal/recurrent meningeal); accessory meningeal and artery of foramen rotundum ↔ inferolateral trunk
- Vidian artery ↔ petrous ICA
Relevant for embolization (stroke, blindness) and collateral flow.

zeilen: Cavernous ICA → basilar (between SCA and AICA)
Most common (0.1–0.5%); associated with aneurysms/AVMs; hypoplastic proximal basilar/VAs
Cervical ICA → basilar via hypoglossal canal
Second most common; often hypoplastic VAs
Cervical ICA/ECA → vertebral between C1 and occiput
cards.notiz: CNBR p. 26–27. Regression order: otic → hypoglossal → trigeminal.

cards.rueckseite: Embryonic hyoid–stapedial remnant from the petrous ICA through the middle ear (stapes) that gives rise to the **MMA**. Imaging: **absent/small foramen spinosum**, enlarged geniculate fossa; can appear as a middle ear mass.

Dominant **anterior radiculomedullary artery** of the thoracolumbar cord: **T9–T12 in ~75%**, from the **left in ~80%**; hairpin turn on angiography as it joins the anterior spinal artery. At risk in left-sided thoracolumbar approaches, aortic surgery, embolization.

cards.vorderseite: Spinal cord blood supply: territories and watershed
cards.rueckseite:
**Anterior spinal artery:** anterior **⅔** of the cord (via sulcal end arteries) → occlusion = **anterior cord syndrome** (dorsal columns spared).
**Paired posterior spinal arteries:** posterior ⅓ (dorsal columns, dorsal horns).
Watershed: **upper/mid thoracic (T1–T4) and around L1**; anterior cord most vulnerable to hypotension/aortic dissection.
